title: Japji at dawn
hookLine: Guru Nanak's Japji is the first morning bani

lines: THE FIRST THING THE DAY HEARS.
cards: Before sunrise in Sikh homes around the world, from Amritsar to Toronto to Nairobi, the same words are being said. A grandfather in a kitchen, murmuring from memory. A student with a small prayer book on her knee.
A taxi driver with a recording playing low. For those who say it, it's the first thing the day hears. And it's the same hymn that opens the Guru Granth Sahib itself.

teach.b: Japji Sahib is by Guru Nanak. Jap means to recite, to repeat, to meditate on; ji and sahib are words of respect. So it's the honored recitation.

It begins with the Mul Mantar, the root verse you know: Ik Onkar, Satnam, one God, whose name is truth. Then a short salok: God was true in the beginning, true through the ages, true now, and will be true.
Then thirty-eight pauris, stanzas, and a closing salok. The first pauri is a surprise. Before telling you how to find God, Guru Nanak tells you what doesn't work.
In paraphrase: thinking won't do it, even a hundred thousand times. Silence won't do it, even if you sit silent forever. Piling up the world's goods won't satisfy hunger.
Thousands upon thousands of clever tricks, and not one goes with you. So how?
The stanza closes with the answer: by walking in the hukam, the Divine Order, the Will, which is written with us.
From there, Japji travels through the whole of life: listening, trusting, the vastness of creation, and at the end five realms of the spirit, rising to the realm of truth.

teach.h: AIR THE GURU, EARTH THE MOTHER.
teach.b: The last salok, in paraphrase, calls air the guru, water the father, the great earth the mother, and day and night the two nurses in whose laps the whole world plays.
One unusual detail: nearly every hymn in the Granth is set to a raag, a musical mode, for singing.
Japji isn't. It's meant to be recited: plain spoken words at the start of the day.

how: Japji Sahib is the first bani of the Sikh morning; many Sikhs recite it from memory or from a gutka in the amrit vela, and it opens the Guru Granth Sahib.

o: a short blessing said before meals
Guru Nanak's hymn that opens the scripture
a sung evening hymn in a musical mode

games.q: what's inside Japji — tap the pairs.
p: air the guru, earth the mother

s: Japji is sung in a raag like most hymns in the Granth
it's one of the few not set to a raag: it's meant to be recited.
Japji's first pauri says thinking alone won't reach God
not even a hundred thousand times; the answer is walking in the hukam.
Japji comes from late in the Guru Granth Sahib
it's on the very first pages.

games.q: Japji's first pauri: thinking fails, silence fails, piling up goods fails. what does Guru Nanak offer instead?
o: walking in the hukam, the Divine Will.
a pilgrimage to a holy river.
games.why: by walking in the hukam, the Divine Order written with us. that answer runs through all of Japji.

practice: If you can, play a recording of Japji Sahib and listen to the first minute or two, the Mul Mantar and the start of the first pauri; you don't need to understand the Punjabi.
Let the sound be the first thing in this moment, the way it is for many Sikhs at dawn. If you can't play it, sit quietly and hear in your mind the two words you already know: Ik Onkar.

wordCard.voice: Japji Sahib. Guru Nanak's recitation, page one of the Guru Granth Sahib, the first bani of the Sikh morning, said at dawn.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: jap, recite or meditate; the heading of Japji on the Granth's first page.

carryVoice: Your line: begin with japji. Page one, the first voice of the day. Day one hundred twenty-nine, done.

sources.ref: Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 1 (Japji, pauri 1: sochai soch na hovai)
Guru Granth Sahib, Ang 8 (closing salok: pavan guru pani pita)
